title: Mapping and Analytics Using UAS
text:
Course Goals
By the end of this course, students will:
Use UAS as a scientific instrument for high-resolution mapping and analysis. Plan, run, and document a UAS mapping mission while following FAA Part 107 rules. Process UAS imagery using Agisoft Metashape, WebODM, and GRASS. Apply UAS-derived data to problems in natural resources, the environment, and the built environment. Develop reproducible workflows and follow ethical practice in UAS data collection and analysis.

Course-Level Learning Objectives
By the end of GIS/MEA 584, students will be able to:

(Apply) Plan and run (or simulate) a UAS mapping mission that follows FAA Part 107 and meets stated accuracy requirements.
(Apply) Process raw UAS imagery into georeferenced orthomosaics, digital surface models, and point clouds using Agisoft Metashape, WebODM, and GRASS.
(Analyze) Evaluate UAS-derived products against reference data using positional and surface accuracy metrics.
(Evaluate) Compare UAS Structure from Motion, airborne lidar, and fused datasets, and recommend an appropriate data source for a stated objective.
(Create) Design a complete UAS analysis workflow, from acquisition through interpretation, for a domain-specific problem and present the results in a project portfolio.

Temporal data framework

space-time dataset may represent a dynamic process

title: Assignment 5A
text:
Workflow
First we need to evaluate the DSMs to find out which are suitable for fusion

Compute the difference between a selected lidar DSM and selected UAS DSMs: entire raster, along a stable linear feature (road and roof).
Use the results to evaluate whether there is a significant systematic error, such as vertical shift in profiles along the road.
Use the raster differences to identify distortions, look for unexpected patterns, verify with profile, and exclude distorted areas from study area.
You have lidar DEM, DSM and a low-distortion subset of UAS DSM:

Create a new DSM for the entire area using two approaches and compare how the two approaches work for water flow modeling.
Combine parts of UAS and lidar DEM to create bare ground, model water flow and compare with water flow modeled on DSM.



1. Analyze the difference between the lidar and UAS DSM
Download the suggested color table for differences, used in the workflow as dif_lidar_uav.txt.
If you run r.colors from command line, make sure the color table file is in your current working directory.
 -40 red
 -1 orange
 -0.5 yellow
 -0.1 grey
 0 white
 0.1 grey
 0.5 cyan
 1 aqua
 35 blue
Download lidar DSM and DEMs if you haven’t done already, unzip it in your working directory and unpack:
r.unpack -o input=mid_pines_lidar2013_dsm.pack
r.unpack -o input=mid_pines_lidar2013_dem.pack
Compute the differences between the lidar and UAS DSMs and evaluate their spatial distribution and
summary statistical properties:
g.region rast=mid_pines_lidar2013_dsm -p
r.mapcalc "diff_lidardsm_agi_june = mid_pines_lidar2013_dsm - 2015_06_20_DSM_agi_11GCP"
r.colors diff_lidardsm_agi_june rules=dif_lidar_uav.txt
r.univar diff_lidardsm_agi_june
r.mapcalc "diff_lidardsm_pix4d_june = mid_pines_lidar2013_dsm - 2015_06_20_pix4d_11GCP_dsm"
r.colors diff_lidardsm_pix4d_june rules=dif_lidar_uav.txt
r.univar diff_lidardsm_pix4d_june
Evaluate possible systematic shift along stable features using the following commands:
r.profile -g input=diff_lidardsm_agi_june output=road.txt coordinates=637208,219491,637059,219734
v.in.ascii input=road.txt output=profile_road separator=space columns="x double,y double,profile double,diff double"
v.univar map=profile_road column=diff
For more visual comparison use GUI Profile Tool.

In Map Display toolbar, find Analyze map - Profile surface map and select raster maps mid_pines_lidar2013_dsm, 2015_06_20_DSM_agi_11GCP, and 2015_06_20_pix4d_11GCP_dsm.
In Profile toolbar, use the second tool Draw transect in map display window and then click in Map Display on the road where you want to start the profile and then where you want to end it.
Use Plot options to show legend and to set colors of the DSM profiles (look for the yellow wheel icon).







Warning



Why are the distortions / errors low along the road but high in the fields?


Because the shift in the lidar and UAS DSM is small we will ignore it in our first set of fusion examples, but we will use the analysis above to select the region with minimal distortion in the UAS DSM and compute a clipped DSM:
g.region n=219720.9 s=219257.1 w=636762.9 e=637190.4 res=0.3 -p
r.mapcalc "2015_06_20_DSM_agi_11GCP_cl = 2015_06_20_DSM_agi_11GCP"


2. Patch and fuse the lidar and UAS DSM
For the rest of the assignment we will use rasters 2015_06_20_DSM_agi_11GCP_cl, mid_pines_lidar2013_dsm, and mid_pines_lidar2013_dem. To make the instructions more readable, we will create a copy of these rasters with short names:
g.copy raster=2015_06_20_DSM_agi_11GCP_cl,uas
g.copy raster=mid_pines_lidar2013_dsm,lidar_dsm
g.copy raster=mid_pines_lidar2013_dem,lidar_dem
Patch UAS DSM with lidar DSM to cover the entire Mid Pines study area and use shaded relief to check for edges:
g.region rast=lidar_dsm -p
r.patch uas,lidar_dsm out=lid_uas_patch
r.relief lid_uas_patch out=lid_uas_patch_relief zscale=5
We have visible discontinuity along the patch edges. Therefore we will use weighted average to smooth out the overlap with the following workflow. We will use two different overlap widths — 5 and 20 meters — compare the results and try to explain how the smoothing works in your report:
r.grow.distance -n input=uas distance=distance
r.mapcalc "patched_smooth_5 = if(distance > 5, uas, if(distance == 0, lidar_dsm, (1 - distance/5) * lidar_dsm + (distance/5 * uas)))"
r.mapcalc "patched_smooth_20 = if(distance > 20, uas, if(distance == 0, lidar_dsm, (1 - distance/20) * lidar_dsm + (distance/20 * uas)))"
r.relief patched_smooth_5 out=patched_smooth_5_relief zscale=5
r.relief patched_smooth_20 out=patched_smooth_20_relief zscale=5


3. Create bare ground by fusing UAS DSM and lidar DEM
To properly model water flow on the UAS DSM, we replace vegetation captured in the DSM with lidar bare ground (lidar_dem). We extract only those parts of UAS DSM where it is higher than lidar ground by 30 cm:
g.region rast=uas -p
r.mapcalc "uas_ground = if(uas - lidar_dem < 0.3, uas, null())"
Now we will fuse lidar and the UAS ground using the same method as above. This time, we will use addon r.patch.smooth:
g.extension r.patch.smooth
In the first case we will use overlap width 10m:
g.region rast=lidar_dsm -p
r.patch.smooth input_a=uas_ground input_b=lidar_dem output=lidar_uas_ground_smooth smooth_dist=10
r.relief lidar_uas_ground_smooth out=lidar_uas_ground_smooth_relief zscale=5
In the second case we will use an alternative approach (using -s flag) which uses spatially variable overlap width based on the elevation differences along the borders (see r.patch.smooth manual):
r.patch.smooth -s input_a=uas_ground input_b=lidar_dem output=lidar_uas_ground_smooth2 overlap=overlap transition_angle=1.3 parallel_smoothing=13
r.relief lidar_uas_ground_smooth2 out=lidar_uas_ground_smooth2_relief zscale=5
Add raster overlap to see the spatially variable overlap.


4. Compare surface flow pattern on patched and fused DSMs
The aim of the processing is to investigate the flow pattern simulated on different DSMs and DEMs. The lidar 2013 and the timeseries of UAS-based DSMs will be used as input for simulations using r.sim.water.
First, we examine the watershed boundaries to see which area to include:
g.region rast=lidar_dem -p
r.watershed elevation=lidar_dem threshold=50000 accumulation=flowacc basin=basin
r.to.vect -t input=basin output=basin type=area
We will compute water flow on our fused DEM within our selected region. We need first order spatial derivatives which can be derived either using r.slope.aspect or during interpolation phase with v.surf.rst.
g.region n=219728.7 s=219435 w=636708.9 e=637122.6 res=0.3 -pa
r.slope.aspect elevation=lid_uas_patch dx=lid_uas_patch_dx dy=lid_uas_patch_dy
The simulation writes water depth and discharge raster maps so we can look at first results soon although the simulation takes a lot of time. Depending on your processing power, you can make the region smaller.
r.sim.water -t elevation=lid_uas_patch dx=lid_uas_patch_dx dy=lid_uas_patch_dy rain_value=30 man_value=0.15 depth=lid_uas_patch_depth discharge=lid_uas_patch_disch nwalkers=100000 niterations=20 output_step=1 hmax=0.2 halpha=8.0 hbeta=1.0
Now we will compute the water flow simulation on the DSM patched using smooth fusion:
r.slope.aspect elevation=patched_smooth_20 dx=patched_smooth_20_dx dy=patched_smooth_20_dy
r.sim.water -t elevation=patched_smooth_20 dx=patched_smooth_20_dx dy=patched_smooth_20_dy rain_value=30 man_value=0.15 depth=patched_smooth_20_depth discharge=patched_smooth_20_disch nwalkers=100000 niterations=20 output_step=1 hmax=0.2 halpha=8.0 hbeta=1.0
Now compare the results (lid_uas_patch_depth.20 and patched_smooth_20_depth.20) at the edge of the datasets.
Finally, we will simulate water flow on the bare ground fused from UAV DSM and lidar DEM:
r.slope.aspect elevation=lidar_uas_ground_smooth dx=lidar_uas_ground_smooth_dx dy=lidar_uas_ground_smooth_dy
r.sim.water -t elevation=lidar_uas_ground_smooth dx=lidar_uas_ground_smooth_dx dy=lidar_uas_ground_smooth_dy rain_value=30 man_value=0.15 depth=ground_depth discharge=ground_disch nwalkers=100000 niterations=20 output_step=1 hmax=0.2 halpha=8.0 hbeta=1.0
Compare ground_depth.20 with the previous results.

Animation and visualisation the results

The formula to calculate GSD is:
\[
\text{GSD} = \frac{\text{A} \times \text{S}}{\text{F} \times \text{D}}

section: What comes home from the field
text:
What comes home from the field


Three things: images, a flight log or EXIF positions, and ground control coordinates. Everything else is computed


The better these three inputs, the less cleanup later. The rest of this section takes them one at a time.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Digital imagery


Usually on the camera’s SD card
Often geotagged: the camera position is written into each photo’s EXIF header
Geotags are the position of the camera, not of anything in the picture, and are accurate to meters unless the aircraft has RTK or PPK
Look through them before processing: blurred, over-exposed, and takeoff frames go


Reminder from 2A: a geotag gets the model into the right neighborhood and seeds the alignment; centimeter accuracy comes from RTK/PPK positions or ground control. The pre-processing step nobody likes is culling bad frames, and it pays off more than any setting in the software.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Focal length and perspective







A short focal length close to the subject gives full perspective: objects near the camera look much larger, scale varies across the frame, distortion grows toward the edges. A longer focal length farther away approaches weak perspective, where rays are nearly parallel and scale is nearly uniform. UAS mapping sits between the two: wide action cameras push toward full perspective, higher flights with a longer lens toward weak perspective. Flight height and lens choice both matter for geometry, and overlap is still what makes the solution robust.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Flight log





The onboard IMU and GNSS receiver log position and attitude for every photo
Written to a text file, or straight into the photos’ EXIF (most DJI aircraft)
Contains the elements of exterior orientation
Describes the camera, not the ground: the model still needs tie points and control to fit the world



Flight attitude: the aircraft’s orientation in space, yaw, pitch, and roll


Logs seed the alignment and then bundle adjustment tightens them. When positions live in EXIF, Metashape reads them automatically; when they are in a separate log you import them with the right column order, time offset, and coordinate system, then check that the cameras land on top of your site.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
GCP coordinates



Surveyed coordinates of targets placed before the flight, or of photo-identifiable points surveyed later
Anchor the model to a coordinate system and let you measure its accuracy
Record the coordinate reference system you surveyed in, every time





GCP placement and the GCP versus checkpoint distinction were in Lecture 2A; here the point is bookkeeping. A GCP file without its CRS is a set of numbers, not coordinates, and mixed CRS is the most common cause of a model that lands hundreds of meters from where it should.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Coordinate reference systems











Geographic (GCS)
Projected (PCS)




Units
degrees
meters or feet


Example
WGS 84 (EPSG:4326)
NC State Plane, NAD83(2011): EPSG:6543 in feet, EPSG:3358 in meters


Use
geotags, raw GNSS
measurement, DEMs, GIS analysis











Vertical datum: GNSS heights are ellipsoidal; maps use orthometric heights above the geoid. In North Carolina the two differ by about 30 m


Geotags arrive in WGS 84 degrees; the products should leave in a projected system with meters, which for our work is NC State Plane. The vertical datum trips up more projects than the horizontal one: if the GCPs are orthometric and the cameras ellipsoidal, the block fits at the wrong height until Metashape is told which is which. Assignment 2B walks through setting both.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Products

Section transition. Four products come out of the pipeline; students met them in 1A and 2A, so this is a quick pass with the emphasis on what each one is good for.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
What comes out of processing


Orthomosaic as the basemap, DSM or DTM as the analysis surface, point cloud as the raw 3D evidence, textured model for visualization, and the report as the record of how good all of it is.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Orthomosaic



Aerial imagery corrected for perspective and terrain so that scale is uniform
A raster with red, green, and blue bands, georeferenced like any other
Metashape calls it an orthomosaic; orthophoto is the generic term





Every pixel is in the right place for measurement, as long as the surface it was draped on is right. Errors in the DSM show up as smeared building edges and doubled features; errors in control show up as the whole map being shifted.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Digital surface model

DSM, digital surface model: the visible surface, including trees, buildings, and cars
DTM or DEM, digital terrain model: bare earth
SfM produces a DSM by default; a DTM needs ground classification and filtering



The distinction matters for every later topic: canopy height is DSM minus DTM, hydrology needs the DTM, and comparing an SfM DSM to a lidar DTM is a classic wrong conclusion. Metashape can classify ground points in the point cloud and build a DTM from those only.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Point cloud



A set of points with x, y, z, usually color, sometimes a class
Represents the external surface of everything the cameras saw
Vector or raster? Neither quite: “a point cloud is a badly behaved raster” (Dale Lutz)





Treat it as raw geometric evidence: classify it, thin it, grid it to a surface. Exported as LAS, LAZ, or COPC it moves into GRASS and other tools for the terrain topics.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Orientation and control

Lecture 2A covered the concepts; this is the checklist form. The historical column is worth a sentence: classical orthorectification needed a DEM as input, and SfM turned that requirement into an output, which is the reason it needs so much overlap.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Exterior orientation


Six elements for every photo: the camera position (X, Y, Z) and its angular orientation:



Photogrammetry
Aviation
Axis
Motion




omega
Roll
x, flight direction
wing tilt side to side


phi
Pitch
y

kappa
Yaw
z

Logs and EXIF provide first guesses for all six; bundle adjustment refines them until the tie points fit to a fraction of a pixel. In the Metashape reference pane these are the camera rows; their accuracy setting tells the adjustment how much to trust them.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Interior orientation



The camera model: focal length, principal point, and lens distortion coefficients
In the past: a laboratory calibration report for a metric camera
Now: self-calibration, estimated from the images during alignment





Self-calibration is what lets a consumer camera produce usable maps, and it is also a source of the doming error from 2A: with weak geometry the adjustment can trade focal length against a bowed surface and still fit. GCPs and a second flying height constrain it. The report prints the solved camera model with its uncertainties.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Ground control points in processing



A marker in Metashape is a GCP: known X, Y, Z plus its projections placed on the photos
Used to set the coordinate system, to optimize the alignment, and to measure error
Checkpoints are markers left unchecked in the reference pane: they are measured, not fitted





Placing targets at Lake Wheeler




Marker placement is the manual part of the workflow and Assignment 2B walks through it: import the coordinates, filter photos by marker, drag the flag onto the target in several photos, optimize. The report then lists control error and checkpoint error separately; students should be able to say which one they would quote.

text:
Processing in Metashape

The real questions: budget and equipment, how often you fly, whether you have the training to process, and whether you have the time


This course uses Metashape (licensed for every student) and WebODM (free). RealityScan handles aerial blocks too and is free for students, so it is a fair third option for personal projects. Cloud services trade money for time and hide the parameters we spend the rest of this lecture on.

Image-based reconstruction from still images, for aerial and close-range work alike

Version 2.3.2, Professional edition, licensed for every student in this class
User manual, Python API, YouTube channel
Tutorials: orthomosaic and DEM with GCPs, point cloud classification and DTM, DEM-based measurements









Metashape 2.x renamed several steps: the dense cloud is now the point cloud, build mesh is build model, and the orthophoto is the orthomosaic. Older tutorials and videos use the old names; the pipeline is the same. Keep the manual open during the assignment; the appendix has the memory requirements per quality setting.

The model step is optional for mapping; the DEM can be built from the point cloud or straight from depth maps.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Loading photos and positions


Add Photos, then check the reference pane: positions from EXIF load automatically
Import a flight log when positions are not in EXIF: set the column order, coordinate system, and time offset
Set camera accuracy (meters and degrees) to what the aircraft’s GNSS can actually deliver


The picture to expect: cameras in neat flight lines above the footprint of the site. If they are scattered or in the ocean, the CRS or the column order is wrong. Camera accuracy is a weight, not a guess: 3 to 10 m for a standard GNSS, 0.02 to 0.05 m for RTK.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Align photos



Detects features in every image and matches them across overlapping images
Solves camera positions, orientations, and the camera model together (bundle adjustment)
Output: tie points (the sparse cloud) and camera poses


















Accuracy
Highest
High
Medium
Low, Lowest




Images
upscaled 2x
full resolution
downscaled 4x
16x, 64x


Use
small, high-quality sets
the usual choice
large projects
triage




Start at High; drop to Medium only for very large projects, and use Low for a quick check that the block hangs together before placing markers. Reference preselection uses the geotags to decide which pairs to match and saves a lot of time on aerial blocks. If coverage is thin, revisit image quality and overlap rather than the settings.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Bundle adjustment



Non-linear least squares over every camera and every tie point
Minimizes reprojection error: the distance between where a 3D point projects and where the feature was detected
Refines exterior and interior orientation at the same time
Markers with known coordinates strengthen and georeference the solution





The mathematical heart of the workflow, and the reason the report’s tie point statistics matter: a mean reprojection error above about one pixel says the camera model or the matches are poor. Optimize Cameras re-runs the adjustment after markers are placed; everything built before that (point cloud, DEM) must be rebuilt afterwards because the geometry moved.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Build point cloud





Tie points






Point cloud













Quality
Ultra high

1/8, 1/16

Metashape computes a depth map for every image and fuses them into the point cloud. Quality is the setting with the biggest effect on time and memory; the manual’s appendix lists RAM per quality and image count. Medium is the assignment setting so that the lab finishes in class; High is what you would use for a real product.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Depth filtering and editing







Depth filtering
Use when




Mild
Complex geometry with many small foreground details you want to keep


Moderate
In between


Aggressive
Aerial mapping; removes most outliers. The Assignment 2B setting


Disabled
Only for very clean, high-quality imagery




Edit the point cloud afterwards if needed: select and delete stray points, or classify ground points for a DTM
Filter the tie points by reprojection error, reconstruction uncertainty, and image count, then optimize again


Filtering prunes outliers that come from poor texture, noise, and badly focused images. Aggressive is the aerial default; Mild is for objects with fine structure such as vegetation or thin poles. Cleaning tie points before optimization is the cheapest accuracy gain in the whole workflow.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Build model









Setting
Options




Surface type
Height field: aerial and terrain, 2.5D, low memory. Arbitrary: closed objects, 3D, high memory


Source data
Depth maps or point cloud; tie points for a quick preview


Face count
High, Medium, Low, or custom




Optional for mapping: DEM and orthomosaic can be built without a model; build one for a textured 3D product









Height field for anything flown nadir over terrain; arbitrary for the 2A-style objects and for facades. Face count controls memory and export size; generate a detailed master and decimate copies for the web. The assignment still builds a model so that students see the textured product, but a production mapping workflow often skips it.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Editing the model



Close holes: fills gaps left by insufficient overlap; required before any volume calculation, otherwise the volume is meaningless
Decimate: replaces a dense mesh with a lighter one
Filter by connected component size and polygon size to drop floating fragments
Export to an external editor for heavy repairs and import the result





Holes are common in UAS data because weather cuts flights short. Close them before computing volumes; leave them alone otherwise, since interpolated geometry is invented geometry. Filtering by component size is the quickest way to remove floaters over water or sky.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Build texture









Mapping mode
Use




Generic
Any object; as uniform a texture as possible


Adaptive orthophoto
Terrain with buildings: flat areas textured orthographically, vertical faces separately


Orthophoto
Terrain only; most compact, weaker on vertical faces


Spherical, Single camera, Keep uv
Special cases: ball-shaped objects, one photo, existing parameterization



Blending: Mosaic (default) picks the most nadir view per pixel; Average blends all views








For terrain, Adaptive orthophoto or Orthophoto; the rest are for objects. Texture size sets the atlas resolution; 4096 is enough for the assignment. Texture is purely visual and does not affect the DEM or orthomosaic.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Build DEM





Projection: set the output CRS here; the assignment uses NC State Plane, EPSG:3358
Source data: point cloud (all points for a DSM, ground class for a DTM), depth maps, or model
Interpolation: Enabled (default) fills gaps visible in at least one image; Disabled keeps only observed cells and is the honest choice for accuracy checks
Resolution: leave the default, which follows the ground sampling distance



Set the projection once here and the orthomosaic follows it. Point cloud as source with the ground class selected is how Metashape produces a DTM. Turn interpolation off when you want to know where the data really are, on when you need a continuous surface for analysis.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Build orthomosaic









Surface: DEM (the usual choice for mapping) or Model (true orthophoto with building facades handled)
Blending mode: Mosaic (default) divides the imagery into frequency bands and blends each; Average uses a weighted mean of all photos; Disabled takes the most nadir photo per pixel and shows seams
Refine seamlines and the ghosting filter help with moving objects and canopy
Same CRS as the DEM; the orthomosaic can only be built in the DEM’s projection



Mosaic is the right default; Average reduces noise on uniform surfaces but blurs edges; Disabled is a diagnostic to see where seams fall. Building on the model instead of the DEM gives a true orthophoto where building sides do not smear, at the cost of model quality driving the result.

Cloud-optimized formats (COG for rasters, COPC for point clouds) are what the later topics read directly from the web bucket. Camera positions and calibration can also be exported (XML, omega phi kappa text, Bundler) for reuse in other software. Save the project after every stage so a failed step can be rerun without recomputing everything before it.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
The processing report


Always generate it. It contains:

Survey data: image count, flying altitude, ground resolution, coverage area, camera model
Camera calibration with residual plots
Camera locations and error estimates
Ground control point and checkpoint errors, listed separately
Overlap map, DEM and orthomosaic previews, processing parameters









Quote the checkpoint RMSE: control point error is circular, the adjustment was told to fit those points


Assignment 2B asks students to explain the report, and this slide is the reading guide. Overlap map: dark areas with fewer than 3 images are where the reconstruction is weak. Calibration residuals: a systematic pattern means the camera model is not fitting. Control versus checkpoint: if checkpoint error is much larger than control error, the model is over-fitting the control and the distribution or weighting needs work.

title: UAS Imagery Processing
text:
Optimizing with markers



Import marker coordinates and set their coordinate system
Place each marker on several photos (filter photos by marker)
Set marker accuracy (0.005 to 0.05 m) and camera accuracy to realistic values
Optimize Cameras: the adjustment now fits the control
Rebuild the point cloud, DEM, and orthomosaic; the geometry has moved





Batch process: queue the steps with their parameters and let them run unattended; the same steps are available from the Python API for repeatable projects


The step students skip is the last one: after optimization every derived product is stale. Batch processing is how you avoid babysitting a multi-hour job, and the Python API is the same workflow as a script, which becomes useful when you process repeat flights of the same site in the change-detection topic.

title: Assignment 2B
text:
Task
Generate an orthomosaic and a digital surface model (DSM) from UAS photographs in Agisoft Metashape Professional 2.3.2, using ground control points, and explain the processing report the software produces, including the accuracy of your products.
The photos were taken by a Trimble UX5 fixed-wing UAS on September 22, 2016 over the NC State Lake Wheeler Road Field Laboratory (map). Processing can be time consuming, so the lab uses a subset of the flight and images downsampled by 50 percent. That is enough to finish in class; the same steps apply to a full flight at full resolution.
Metashape 2.x renamed several workflow steps. The instructions use the current names, with the older name in parentheses the first time it appears, so that older tutorials and videos still make sense. The screenshots are from Metashape 1.x and may show the old dialog names.
Keep your exported products and the processing report: Assignment 2C processes the same imagery in WebODM and compares the two.

Workflow overview (with GCPs)

Stage 1: load photos and camera positions, align them (a preliminary model to place the GCPs on)
Stage 2: place the GCPs and optimize the alignment
Stage 3: build the point cloud, model, DEM, and orthomosaic
Stage 4: export the products and generate the report

title: Assignment 2B
text:
Preparation

Data

Download the data: photos, the flight log, and the coordinates of 3 GCPs
Or use your own data set, with a flight log or geotags and GCP coordinates



Software

Agisoft Metashape Professional 2.3.2 (installer). A license is provided for every student in this class; the activation instructions are on Moodle.



Preferences
Set these once, the first time you run Metashape; they are kept for later sessions.

Menu > Tools > Preferences
General tab: leave the defaults (optionally enable “Write log to file” to keep a text log of every run).
GPU tab: check “Use CPU when performing GPU accelerated processing” at the bottom. Your GPU, if Metashape detects one, is listed here and should be checked.

Preferences

title: Assignment 2B
text:
Stage 1: Aligning photos
A preliminary alignment is needed before the GCPs can be located on the photos.

Adding photos

Menu > Workflow > Add Photos
Select all the photos in the downloaded folder. They appear in the Reference pane with local coordinates, because the coordinate system has not been set yet.
Click the Settings icon  in the Reference pane toolbar and set the coordinate system to WGS 84 (EPSG:4326).







Note



The Settings dialog also holds the accuracy weights the adjustment uses:

Camera accuracy (m): positional accuracy of the camera geotags, typically 2.5 to 10 m for a standard GNSS receiver, centimeters with RTK or PPK.
Camera accuracy (deg): accuracy of yaw, pitch, and roll; use a large value (2 degrees or more) unless the attitude was measured precisely.
Marker accuracy (m): accuracy of the surveyed GCP coordinates, usually 0.01 to 0.05 m; x/y and z can be set separately.
Scale bar accuracy (m): accuracy of measured distances between markers, often 0.001 m.
Marker accuracy (pix): how precisely a marker can be placed on an image; 0.1 px for printed targets, 0.5 px for natural features.
Tie point accuracy (pix): weight of the automatically detected points, typically 0.5 to 1 px.

For this flight leave the defaults.





Loading camera positions
Click the Import icon  in the Reference pane toolbar and select the camera positions file 2016_09_22_sample.txt.







Note



Metashape reads camera orientation files in .csv, .txt, .tel, .xml, and .log formats. The Trimble Aerial Imaging log is a .jxl file; the provided .txt is a converted copy. To convert your own, use jxl2csv by Vaclav Petras.


Check that the columns are mapped correctly (name, latitude, longitude, altitude, yaw, pitch, roll); the column numbers can be adjusted at the top right of the dialog.


Aligning photos

Menu > Workflow > Align Photos

Accuracy: Low (fast; enough to place the GCPs)
Generic preselection: enabled
Reference preselection: enabled, Source
Key point limit and tie point limit: default
Adaptive camera model fitting: enabled


Click Save  in the toolbar.

title: Assignment 2B
text:
Stage 2: Placing GCPs

Loading the GCP coordinates
Click the Import icon  in the Reference pane toolbar and select the GCP file GCP_3.txt.

Check the column mapping and uncheck Rotation: GCPs are stationary and have no yaw, pitch, or roll.
Metashape asks Can’t find match for ‘UAV 3’ entry. Create new marker? Choose Yes to All; one marker is created for each named GCP in the file, listed in the Reference pane below the cameras.



Placing the markers on the photos
Each GCP now has to be located on every photo that shows it. The instructional video shows the process.
The Model pane shows the approximate marker positions; they are easier to see with cameras hidden (Menu > View > Show/Hide Items > Show Cameras).
 
Right-click a marker in the Reference pane and choose Filter Photos by Marker.

The Photos pane now lists only the images that probably show the selected GCP.






Note



This filter works because the photos are geotagged. With non-geotagged photos, or a site you do not know, build the point cloud or even the model and texture first (the steps in Stage 3) so that the Model pane shows a recognizable preview of the area rather than only tie points.


Double-click a photo thumbnail to open it next to the Model pane. The marker appears as a grey icon ; drag it onto the center of the target.

Once placed, the marker turns into a green flag: it is enabled and will be used in the adjustment.
Repeat on the next photo. After the marker has been placed on two photos, Metashape predicts its position on the remaining photos closely; drag it slightly to enable it (green flag) or leave it grey to exclude that photo.
Filter photos by marker again after each marker: as the positions improve, more photos that show the GCP appear in the Photos pane.
This lab uses 3 GCPs, the mathematical minimum for defining the coordinate system. Reliable error estimates need at least 4, and 5 or more spread across the site, including its center, keep the terrain from tilting or doming. Real projects also withhold some surveyed points as checkpoints to measure the error independently.
Click Save .


Optimizing the alignment
Click View Errors  in the Reference pane to see the current errors. The best results come from optimizing twice: first on the camera coordinates only, then on the GCP markers only.
In the Reference pane, leave all cameras checked and uncheck all markers (select one, press Ctrl+A, right-click, Uncheck), so that this first pass adjusts on the camera coordinates only.
Click Optimize Cameras  in the Reference pane toolbar. In the dialog, check every camera calibration parameter (f, cx, cy, k1 to k4, p1, p2, b1, b2) so that all of them are refined.






Warning



Depending on the Metashape version, the Optimize Cameras icon is a star or a camera with a wrench.




Optimizing on the markers
In the Reference pane:

uncheck all cameras (select one, press Ctrl+A, right-click, Uncheck)
check all markers (select one, press Ctrl+A, right-click, Check)

Click Settings  and leave the default marker accuracy (0.005 m), or enter your GCPs’ surveyed precision if you know it (0.01 to 0.05 m is typical for RTK GNSS).
Click Optimize Cameras  again with the default options, then Save .
View Errors  now shows how much the optimization reduced the marker errors. Note the values: they go in your report.

title: Assignment 2B
text:
Stage 3: Building geometry and products
Before building the point cloud, check the bounding box of the reconstruction: it must contain the whole area of interest in all three dimensions, and should not be much larger, since the box size drives processing time and memory.
Adjust it with the Resize Region  and Rotate Region  tools. The red face of the box must be at the bottom.

The next steps are the slow ones. Run them one at a time, or queue them with batch processing (end of this stage) and let them run unattended.

Menu > Workflow > Build Point Cloud (Build Dense Cloud in Metashape 1.x)

Quality: Medium
Depth filtering: Aggressive








Quality
What it does




Medium
downsamples the images 4x; a 3D point every 4 pixels; the class setting


High
downsamples 2x; typically several hours; good results for most work


Ultra high
a 3D point for every pixel of the original imagery; a day or more









Note



For large data sets, check the memory requirements per quality setting and image count in the appendix of the Metashape manual.



Click Save .


Menu > Workflow > Build Model (Build Mesh in 1.x)

Source data: Point cloud (Dense cloud in 1.x)
Surface type: Height field
Face count: Medium
Advanced options: leave the defaults







Note



A face count of 0 lets Metashape choose, which may not be enough to describe every feature on the terrain. For mapping, the model is optional: the DEM and orthomosaic can be built from the point cloud directly. This lab builds one so that you also get a textured 3D model to export.





Menu > Workflow > Build Texture

Texture type: Diffuse map
Source data: Images
Mapping mode: Orthophoto
Blending mode: Mosaic (default)
Texture size/count: 4096
Enable hole filling: enabled; Enable ghosting filter: disabled

Click Save .



Editing the model
If the image overlap was insufficient, the model has holes. Close them only if you need a watertight model, for example for volume calculations, where 100 percent of holes must be closed.

Menu > Tools > Model > Close Holes (Tools > Mesh in 1.x)
Select the size of the largest hole to close, as a percentage of the model size.






Warning



Do not choose 100 percent unless you are calculating volumes.



This data set has enough overlap to skip the step, but holes are common in UAS data because weather cuts flights short.



Building the DEM

Menu > Workflow > Build DEM
Set the output coordinate system here. Rather than keeping the project’s WGS 84, change it to the system commonly used in North Carolina, NAD83(HARN) / North Carolina in meters, EPSG:3358. Leave source data as Point cloud and interpolation Enabled (default).




Building the orthomosaic

Menu > Workflow > Build Orthomosaic (Build Orthophoto in 1.x)
The orthomosaic takes the DEM’s coordinate system (EPSG:3358) and can only be built in that projection. Leave surface DEM and blending mode Mosaic (default).




Batch processing

Menu > Workflow > Batch Process > Add
Batch processing runs several steps in order without user intervention, with the same parameters as above:

Optimize Cameras (skip if you already optimized in Stage 2)
Build Point Cloud
Build Model
Build Texture
Build DEM
Build Orthomosaic

text:
Assignment

Assignment 1B: UAS Rule Part 107 test subset - see the assignment page for the full instructions and submission details.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Objectives

Understand the role of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) in ensuring safety in the National Airspace System (NAS)
Recognize the main types of UAS operations and the rules for each: Part 107 for commercial use and the 49 USC 44809 recreational exception (TRUST)
Know the Part 107 operating rules, including airspace authorization with LAANC
Recognize permanent and temporary “no-drone-zones”
Understand the Certificate of Authorization (COA) for public agencies and when educational use requires Part 107


Frame the lecture: last week was what UAS are; this week is when and how you may legally fly them.
Emphasize that everyone in the room who ever launches a drone, even a 249 g toy in a park, falls under one of these rule sets. The recreational exception is a statute (49 USC 44809, from the 2018 FAA Reauthorization Act), while commercial rules are regulation (14 CFR Part 107, effective August 29, 2016).
This material changes often; encourage students to always verify against faa.gov/uas rather than blog posts.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)



Created in 1958 in response to a series of fatal accidents and midair collisions involving commercial aircraft
Mandated to develop plans and policies for the use of navigable airspace to ensure the safety of aircraft and the efficient use of airspace
Since the creation of the FAA, American airspace has become one of the most regulated fields in the United States





A Brief History of the FAA


The 1956 Grand Canyon midair collision is the classic trigger event; the Federal Aviation Act of 1958 created the agency. The key takeaway for drone pilots: the FAA owns the airspace from the ground up. There is no unregulated altitude band below 400 ft; that figure is an operating limit, not a boundary of FAA authority.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
National Airspace System (NAS)

Already congested with piloted aircraft, and adding a swarm of UAS requires thoughtful planning
Main mandate: to ensure that UAS do not endanger current users of the NAS nor compromise the safety of people and property on the ground
Most small UAS cannot yet detect and avoid other aircraft, the gap behind many of today’s operating rules and the proposed Part 108 BVLOS rule (end of this lecture)


Detect-and-avoid is the drone equivalent of “see and avoid” that manned pilots perform visually. Because a remote pilot cannot scan the sky from the cockpit, the default mitigations are visual line of sight and yielding right of way. This is the thread that connects most Part 107 operating rules, and the reason beyond-visual-line-of-sight flight currently requires a waiver. Foreshadow the Part 108 slide at the end.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
section: Who may fly, and under which rules?
text:
Who may fly, and under which rules?
Types of UAS operations

Section transition: from the FAA’s mandate to the rule sets it created. The next slides sort every flight into one of three buckets and then work through each bucket’s requirements.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Types of UAS operations



Commercial / civil: any flight in furtherance of a business or non-recreational purpose, under 14 CFR Part 107


Recreational: strictly for personal enjoyment, under the 49 USC 44809 exception



Public aircraft operations: government entities, under Part 107 or a Certificate of Authorization (COA)


Educational use can fall under the recreational exception or Part 107, depending on the activity



Intent decides: the same aircraft can fly recreationally on Saturday and commercially on Monday


The 2018 FAA Reauthorization Act repealed the old “model aircraft” rule (Section 336) and replaced it with the 44809 recreational exception; the FAA no longer uses “model aircraft” as an operational category. Stress that intent, not the aircraft, determines the category: the same Mini 4 Pro is recreational in a park on Saturday and commercial when photographing a field site for a project.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Recreational use of UAS

Operation of an unmanned aircraft strictly for personal interests and enjoyment
Taking photographs for your own personal use is recreational
Taking the same photographs for compensation, for sale, or in furtherance of any business (including research or coursework deliverables for pay) is a commercial operation under Part 107


Useful test question for the class: is posting drone footage to a monetized YouTube channel recreational? (No; compensation makes it commercial.) Is flying to practice piloting skills for a future Part 107 job recreational? (FAA guidance says yes, if the flight itself is purely for enjoyment/proficiency.) The line is the purpose of the individual flight.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
The 44809 exception: conditions
To fly recreationally without a Part 107 certificate you must follow all conditions of 49 USC 44809:



Fly strictly for recreational purposes
Pass TRUST (The Recreational UAS Safety Test) and carry proof of completion
Register the aircraft if it weighs 250 g or more (FAADroneZone) and comply with Remote ID
Follow the safety guidelines of an FAA-recognized Community Based Organization (CBO)





TRUST (required since 2021) is free, online, cannot be failed (wrong answers are corrected and re-asked), and takes about 30 minutes; proof must be shown to the FAA or law enforcement on request. Recognized CBOs include the Academy of Model Aeronautics and FPV Freedom Coalition; their published guidelines fill in operational detail the statute leaves open. Registration is $5 for 3 years and the number goes on the aircraft. Assignment 1B offers TRUST as one of its two options.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
section: The 44809 exception: where you may fly
text:
The 44809 exception: where you may fly



Keep the aircraft within visual line of sight (or use a co-located visual observer)
Give way to and never interfere with manned aircraft
Fly at or below 400 ft in uncontrolled (Class G) airspace
In controlled airspace (Class B, C, D, E surface areas): fly only with a LAANC authorization or FAA authorization, at or below the UAS Facility Map altitude





This slide is where the old rules differ most from current ones: the pre-2019 “notify airports within 5 miles” requirement is gone. Today recreational and commercial pilots use the same LAANC system for controlled-airspace authorization, covered in detail later in this lecture. UAS Facility Maps grid the airspace around airports into maximum authorized altitudes (often 0 ft near the runway ends).

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Recreational use - Do not fly

over people or moving vehicles, and keep a safe distance from individuals and vulnerable property
near or over sensitive infrastructure (power stations, water treatment facilities, correctional facilities, heavily traveled roadways, government facilities)
in adverse weather such as high winds or reduced visibility
under the influence of alcohol or drugs


These practices come from the CBO safety guidelines that the statute requires recreational flyers to follow, and they mirror many Part 107 rules, which makes the later transition to certificated flying easier. Wind is the practical one for mapping students: most small quads struggle above roughly 20 mph sustained wind, well before the flight becomes illegal it becomes useless for data quality.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Recreational use - safety practices

Ensure the operating environment is safe and the operator is competent and proficient
Check and follow all local laws and ordinances before flying over private property
Do not conduct surveillance or photograph persons where there is an expectation of privacy without permission


Privacy is mostly governed by state and local law, not the FAA: North Carolina’s drone statutes (G.S. 15A-300.1) prohibit surveillance of persons or private property without consent, with civil damages available. Good discussion prompt: who enforces what? The FAA handles airspace violations; local police handle privacy, trespass, and harassment complaints.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Flying under Part 107
Commercial operations: the pilot, the aircraft, the rules

Section transition into the course’s home rule set. Structure of this section: what counts as commercial, then pilot requirements, aircraft requirements, operating rules, operations over people, waivers, and accident reporting.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Commercial use of UAS
Any use in connection with a business or work, including:



Selling photos or videos taken from a UAS
Providing contract services, such as industrial equipment or factory inspection
Providing professional services, such as security or telecommunications
Monitoring the progress of work your company is performing
University research and mapping projects like the ones in this course


 


The FAA interprets “commercial” broadly: any flight in furtherance of a business or performed as part of one’s job, whether or not money changes hands for the flight itself. Faculty research flights and most university data-collection missions are Part 107 operations. This is why the flight operations later in this course are conducted under Part 107 by certificated pilots.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Commercial use - Remote Pilot requirements

Must be at least 16 years of age
Be able to read, speak, write, and understand English
Be in a physical and mental condition to safely fly a drone
Pass the initial aeronautical knowledge exam: “Unmanned Aircraft General - Small (UAG)”




Must pass the applicable Transportation Security Administration (TSA) vetting
See the course Step-by-Step Guide to Getting an FAA Part 107 License





The knowledge test is 60 multiple-choice questions, 2 hours, 70% to pass, about $175 at a PSI testing center. Point students to the step-by-step guide on the course site; also note the certificate is not required for this course, but it is one of the most employable single credentials a geospatial student can add. Assignment 1B lets them either take TRUST or work through Part 107 sample test questions.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Remote Pilot Certificate



Must be easily accessible by the remote pilot during all UAS operations
Certificate holders must complete free online recurrent training every 24 calendar months to maintain aeronautical knowledge recency (effective April 2021)
FAA Safety Team Part 107 Small UAS Training Course (login required)





Before April 2021 keeping current meant paying to retake a proctored test every 24 months; now it is free online recurrent training (course ALC-677) that also covers the 2021 night-operations and operations-over-people rules. The certificate itself never expires; only recency lapses, and a lapsed pilot simply completes the training before flying again.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Commercial use - UAS requirements



Must weigh less than 55 lbs
Must be registered in FAADroneZone ($5, valid 3 years)
Must comply with Remote ID
Must undergo a pre-flight check by the remote pilot in command





Under Part 107 every aircraft is registered individually regardless of weight (the 250 g threshold applies only to recreational registration). At 55 lbs and above you leave Part 107 entirely and need an exemption or airworthiness certification. The pre-flight check requirement (107.49) is where checklists, battery inspection, and control-link verification live; this becomes routine in the flight-planning topic.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Part 107: flight limits



Must fly at or below 400 feet above ground level (AGL), or within 400 feet of a structure if flying higher
Must not fly from a moving vehicle unless in a sparsely populated area
Must fly at or below 100 mph (87 knots)
Must yield right of way to manned aircraft





The 400-ft-of-a-structure allowance (107.51) exists for tower and building inspection: you may fly up to 400 ft above a structure’s top while within a 400 ft radius of it. For mapping work in this course, flight altitude is chosen for ground sampling distance and is normally 200-400 ft AGL, so the ceiling rarely binds, but it matters when a site sits under a low LAANC grid altitude.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
section: Part 107: line of sight and night
text:
Part 107: line of sight and night


Must keep the UAS within visual line of sight (VLOS) of the remote pilot in command or a visual observer




Night operations allowed without a waiver (since April 2021) if the pilot has completed current training and the aircraft has anti-collision lighting visible for 3 statute miles


VLOS means unaided eyes (glasses fine, binoculars or FPV goggles alone do not count); an FPV pilot needs a visual observer next to them. The 2021 rule ended the era of night waivers: before it, daylight-only operation (old 107.29) was the most-waived rule in Part 107. Thermal mapping missions, which fly at night or dawn for temperature contrast, are the course-relevant beneficiary.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Remote ID

UAS must broadcast identification, location, and control-station location during flight (rule effective 2021, enforced since March 16, 2024)
Three ways to comply:

Standard Remote ID aircraft (built-in broadcast)
Aircraft with an attached broadcast module (VLOS only)
Fly without Remote ID only inside an FAA-Recognized Identification Area (FRIA)

Applies to all aircraft that must be registered (recreational and Part 107)


Think of Remote ID as a digital license plate broadcast over WiFi/Bluetooth that anyone with a phone app can receive; the FAA and law enforcement can correlate it with registration data. FRIAs are fixed sites sponsored by CBOs and educational institutions, mostly model-aircraft fields. Practical note for the course: all recent DJI aircraft have standard Remote ID built in; check compliance for anything older or self-built.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Operations over people: Categories 1-4
Since April 2021, routine flight over people is allowed under Part 107 if the aircraft qualifies for one of four categories (14 CFR Part 107 Subpart D).



Category
Aircraft limit
Certification
Over people




1
Under 250 g
Self-declared
Routine


2
11 ft-lbs impact
Manufacturer DOC
Routine


3
25 ft-lbs impact
Manufacturer DOC
Restricted sites only


4
None
Airworthiness certificate
Per certificate






Not airspace classes: Category 1-4 describes the aircraft; Class B-G describes the airspace


Set up the next two slides. Before 2021 any flight over a person outside your crew required a waiver; the Operations Over People rule made it routine, scaled to how much harm the aircraft could do. Emphasize the terminology trap: FAA “Category 1-4” (over-people) vs airspace “Class B-G”; the exam uses both. Also distinguish transiting over people (allowed per category) from sustained hovering over crowds.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Category 1
Eligibility: aircraft weighs 0.55 lb (250 g) or less, including everything attached.
Requirements:

No exposed rotating parts that could lacerate human skin
Remote ID required for sustained flight over open-air assemblies

Operations:

May fly over people without a waiver or a Declaration of Compliance

Example UAS: sub-250 g aircraft such as the DJI Mini series or DJI Neo (with propeller guards where needed to meet the laceration requirement)

Category 1 is self-declared: no FAA paperwork, the operator just has to be right about the weight and the laceration criterion. This is a major reason the sub-250 g market segment exists; manufacturers engineer to sit under the threshold. Weight includes payload, so adding a prop-guard set or beacon can push an aircraft out of Category 1. This is the category students will actually use.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Categories 2, 3, and 4
Categories 2 and 3: no weight limit; injury-severity based, demonstrated through an FAA-accepted Means of Compliance and a manufacturer Declaration of Compliance (DOC)

Category 2: impact must not exceed 11 ft-lbs of kinetic energy; no exposed lacerating parts; routine flight over people
Category 3: impact must not exceed 25 ft-lbs; no flight over open-air assemblies; over people only within a closed or restricted-access site with notice, or when people are under cover or in stationary vehicles

Category 4: aircraft holds an airworthiness certificate under Part 21, operated within its flight manual with a maintenance, inspection, and record-keeping program; may operate over open-air assemblies per the certificate

Categories 2 and 3 are manufacturer-certified, not operator-declared, and as of the mid-2020s very few aircraft hold accepted Declarations of Compliance, so these categories are rare in practice. The kinetic-energy thresholds translate to roughly a 2 lb and 4 lb aircraft at terminal velocity, though the tests are on impact severity, not weight. Category 4 is the “certify it like an airplane” path aimed at larger aircraft and delivery-style operations; no common survey drone uses it. The practical takeaway hierarchy: Category 1 if under 250 g, otherwise plan missions so you are not over people at all, which is standard practice for site mapping.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Waivers from Part 107 operating rules

To operate outside Part 107 rules, apply for a Certificate of Waiver through FAADroneZone
The FAA grants waivers when the proposed operation can be performed safely with the applicant’s proposed mitigations


The waiver process asks “how will you mitigate the risk this rule addresses?” and successful applications read like safety cases, not requests. Approval times run weeks to months, so waivers are planned mission infrastructure, not a quick fix. Since the 2021 rules absorbed night operations and some over-people flight, the dominant remaining waiver is beyond visual line of sight.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Waivable sections of Part 107



Operation from a moving vehicle or aircraft (§ 107.25)
Visual line of sight aircraft operation (§ 107.31) - the most requested waiver today (BVLOS)
Visual observer (§ 107.33)
Operation of multiple small unmanned aircraft systems (§ 107.35)



Yielding the right of way (§ 107.37(a))
Operation over people (§ 107.39, beyond the category rules)
Operation in certain airspace (§ 107.41)
Operating limitations for small unmanned aircraft (§ 107.51)



No waiver will be issued to allow the carriage of property of another by aircraft for compensation or hire


BVLOS (107.31) waivers dominate because they unlock the economics of linear inspection, agriculture, and delivery: one pilot covering miles instead of a visual bubble. Daylight-only operation (old 107.29) used to top this list before the 2021 night rule removed the need. The carriage-for-hire exclusion is why drone delivery companies operate under separate exemptions and air-carrier rules, not Part 107 waivers.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Accident reporting (§ 107.9)
No later than 10 days after an operation, the remote pilot in command must report to the FAA any operation of the small unmanned aircraft involving at least:



Serious injury to any person or any loss of consciousness; or
Damage to any property, other than the small unmanned aircraft, unless the cost of repair (including materials and labor) or fair market value of the property does not exceed $500





Reports go through FAADroneZone. Note what does not trigger a report: destroying your own aircraft, or minor property damage under $500. “Serious injury” follows the AIS Level 3 standard, roughly an injury requiring hospitalization. Universities typically layer their own incident reporting on top, which connects to the NC State UAS procedures linked from the part page.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Where can you fly?
Airspace classes, LAANC, and reading the chart

Section transition into airspace. This is the most practical section of the lecture: every mission starts with “what airspace is my site under and do I need authorization?”

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Airspace classes

U.S. airspace classes in profile
Class B/C/D and Class E surface areas: operations require an airspace authorization, normally obtained through LAANC
Class G (uncontrolled): may operate while following all other Part 107 rules, no authorization needed


Walk through the airspace classes on the figure from the top down: A (18,000 ft and above, irrelevant to sUAS), B around major hubs like Charlotte, C around mid-size towered airports like RDU, D around smaller towered airports, E controlled airspace that can extend to the surface, G uncontrolled. The practical question for every mission: is my site under controlled airspace that reaches the surface? If yes, get a LAANC authorization first.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
LAANC - airspace authorization
Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability



Automated, near-real-time FAA authorization for flights in controlled airspace, up to the altitude in the UAS Facility Maps
Available to both Part 107 and recreational flyers
Request through an FAA-approved service supplier app (e.g. Aloft, AutoPylot, Airspace Link)
Above facility-map altitudes or where LAANC is unavailable: apply via FAADroneZone





LAANC replaced the old call-the-tower and 5-mile-notification era: since 2018-2019 authorization is an app workflow that usually returns approval in seconds. Demo one supplier app live if possible, showing the UAS Facility Map grid around RDU: each grid cell shows the maximum altitude the FAA will auto-authorize, and zero-grid cells require a manual FAADroneZone application with longer lead time. This is the single most-used regulatory tool students will touch in practice.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Reading aeronautical charts
Solid lines and blue mean more restrictive; dashed lines and magenta mean less restrictive:








Airspace class
Chart symbol
Around




B
Solid blue
Major hubs (Charlotte)


C
Solid magenta
Mid-size towered airports (RDU)


D
Dashed blue
Smaller towered airports


E (surface)
Dashed magenta
Non-towered airports with instrument approaches



Interactive charts: VFRMap, SkyVector | FAA course on airspace classification

Chart reading is heavily tested on the Part 107 exam, so this slide maps directly to Assignment 1B question types. Suggest pulling up SkyVector on the Raleigh area and having students identify the RDU Class C shelves and the dashed magenta Class E surface areas nearby. Remind them that the sectional shows airspace; the UAS Facility Map shows what LAANC will authorize, and both are needed for mission planning.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Airports and controlled airspace

No 5-mile rule: airspace class, not distance to an airport, decides whether you need authorization (the pre-2019 notification requirement was repealed with Section 336)




Both recreational and Part 107 pilots need a LAANC (or FAADroneZone) authorization to fly in Class B, C, D, or surface Class E airspace
Authorization is granted up to the UAS Facility Map altitude for the grid cell; near runways this is often 0 ft (no automatic authorization)





Called out explicitly because the 5-mile rule persists in older videos and blog posts and in some exam-prep material. The current logic is airspace-based, not distance-based: a site 4 miles from an airport in Class G needs nothing, while a site 8 miles away under a Class C shelf that reaches the surface needs authorization. Always resolve the question with a facility-map app, not distance.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Where NOT to fly

FAA “No Drone Zone” outreach signage
Transition into airspace restrictions. The no-drone-zone signage is public outreach; the legal substance is in the TFRs, special-use airspace, and security restrictions on the following slides. Best pre-flight habit: check a LAANC/B4UFLY-service app the day of the flight, since restrictions appear and move (wildfires, VIP movement, sporting events).

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Airspace restrictions

Security Sensitive Airspace Restrictions
Temporary Flight Restrictions (TFRs)
Restricted or Special Use Airspace
Stadiums and sporting events
Wildfires


Preview the taxonomy: some restrictions are permanent and mapped (special use airspace, security areas), some are scheduled (stadium TFRs), some pop up with hours’ notice (wildfire TFRs). All of them override any LAANC authorization you may hold. The next slides take them one at a time.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Security sensitive airspace restrictions



All UAS flights prohibited within the airspace
Restrictions extend from the ground up to 400 feet AGL
Apply to all types and purposes of UAS flight operations
Remain in effect 24 hours a day, 7 days a week



14 CFR § 99.7


These cover sites like military bases, national landmarks, and critical infrastructure designated at federal request. They are depicted on the FAA’s UAS-specific maps rather than sectionals, another reason to check a drone-specific app rather than only a pilot’s chart. Violations here draw federal attention quickly; some sites have counter-UAS authority.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Temporary flight restrictions (TFRs)



TFR: airspace where flight is limited because of a temporary hazardous condition (wildfire, chemical spill) or a security-related event (VIP movement, large public events)


The TFR text gives the details: size, altitude, effective times, and which operations are restricted or permitted





TFR map, TFR list


Presidential TFRs are the famous ones: a 30-nautical-mile ring that shuts down drone activity wherever the President travels, often on short notice. For fieldwork the operational lesson is to check TFRs the same day as the flight; a site that was clear during planning can be closed by a wildfire TFR the morning of the mission.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Restricted or special use airspace


Types of Special Use Airspace include:

Prohibited areas
Restricted areas
Warning areas
Military operation areas (MOAs)
Alert areas
Controlled firing areas (CFAs)



The airspace surrounding Washington DC is the most restricted in the country More info


Prohibited areas (P-56 over the White House and National Mall) ban flight outright; restricted areas require permission from the using agency; MOAs and warning areas are legal but hazardous. North Carolina relevance: large MOAs and restricted areas sit east of Raleigh around Seymour Johnson AFB and the Dare County bombing range, which matters for coastal mapping projects.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Stadiums and sporting events


UAS operations are prohibited within a radius of 3 nautical miles of the stadium or venue, from one hour before to one hour after, for:

Major League Baseball
National Football League
NCAA Division One Football
NASCAR Cup Series, IndyCar, and Champ Series races





This is a standing TFR up to 3,000 ft AGL. Local hook: Carter-Finley Stadium is on this list on football Saturdays, and the restriction covers a 3 nm radius, which reaches much of west Raleigh including parts of campus and Lake Wheeler Road. Check the game schedule before planning fall field days.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Wildfires


It is illegal to fly your UAS in or around a wildfire firefighting operation 




“If you fly, we can’t” is the fire community’s campaign line: a single drone sighting grounds firefighting aircraft. Wildfire TFRs carry civil penalties that can exceed $20,000 plus potential criminal liability. The legitimate path exists: public agencies fly fire-mapping missions under COAs in coordination with incident command, an application area from Lecture 1A.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Beyond Part 107
Public agencies, COAs, and educational use

Section transition: the rule paths that are not Part 107. Most students will never file a COA, but many will work for or with agencies that hold one.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Public entities


Publicly funded universities, law enforcement agencies, fire departments, and other government agencies have two options:

Follow the same requirements and operating rules as commercial users (Part 107)

OR

Operate as public aircraft under a blanket Certificate of Authorization (COA)





In practice most public entities, including most university flight programs, simply use Part 107 because it is simpler and their missions fit within it; COAs are reserved for operations Part 107 cannot cover, such as certain law-enforcement or emergency operations. Ask the class why an agency might still want a COA (self-certification of pilots, emergency provisions, operations outside Part 107 limits).

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Certificate of Authorization
Can be obtained:

Only by government entities, such as federal and state agencies, law enforcement, and public colleges and universities, for public (governmental) UAS aircraft operations

Allows:

Flights at or below 400 feet in Class G airspace nationwide, self-certification of the UAS pilot, and emergency COAs under special circumstances

Applying:

Online via the FAA’s COA process (sample application); average processing under 60 days, expedited in emergency and life-threatening situations


The blanket public COA is the standing nationwide authorization; operations outside it (higher altitudes, specific controlled airspace) need a jurisdictional COA for a defined area. Self-certification of pilots is the notable difference from Part 107: the agency, not the FAA, attests pilot qualification. Students will not file COAs themselves, but they may work under one; emergency COAs matter after disasters, as with post-hurricane mapping flights in North Carolina coordinated with emergency management.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Educational use



Under 49 USC 44809(c) and FAA educational-user guidance, students at accredited institutions may fly under the recreational exception as part of coursework (TRUST, registration, and all other 44809 conditions still apply)
Faculty-directed research and flights that further university business generally require Part 107


In this course: instructional flight operations are conducted under Part 107 by certificated pilots


 


History for context: a May 2016 FAA legal interpretation first allowed student flying under model-aircraft rules; the 2018 Reauthorization Act wrote the concept into statute at 44809(c), and 2021 FAA guidance details when instructors and faculty can participate (limited assistance is fine; directing research flights is not recreational). The safe institutional default is Part 107 for anything tied to funded research.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
UAS best practices



If you can, tell other people you’ll be taking pictures or video of them before you do so
If someone has a reasonable expectation of privacy, don’t violate it by taking pictures or video, unless you’ve got a very good reason
Don’t fly over other people’s private property without permission if you can easily avoid doing so
Don’t harass people with your drone



Don’t gather personal data for no reason, and don’t keep it for longer than you have to
If you keep sensitive data about other people, secure it against loss or theft
If someone asks you to delete personal data about him or her that you’ve gathered, do so, unless you’ve got a good reason not to




These come from the NTIA voluntary best practices for UAS privacy: not law, but the professional norm, and often stricter than what the FAA requires. For mapping projects, landowner permission for takeoff, landing, and ground control points is both courteous and usually a practical necessity; the FAA governs the air, but the launch site is property law. The data-handling side maps directly onto research-data management: orthophotos of residential areas contain personal data (faces, vehicles, backyards), and IRB or data-management plans may govern retention. Good habit to teach: plan flight lines to minimize capture of areas outside the study site rather than cropping afterwards.

title: UAS Rules and Regulations
text:
Current developments - BVLOS and Part 108

The biggest open problem in UAS regulation today: beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) flight without a waiver
The FAA published the proposed Part 108 rule (Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, August 2025) to enable routine BVLOS operations
Built on automated traffic awareness/deconfliction services and aircraft airworthiness acceptance instead of one-off waivers


The rules keep moving: always verify against faa.gov/uas before you fly


Close the loop with the detect-and-avoid concern from the NAS slide: Part 108 is the FAA’s answer, replacing case-by-case BVLOS waivers with a performance-based rule using strategic deconfliction and third-party services. Check the current rulemaking status before lecture and update the class, since the final rule may land during or after this semester. Good discussion prompt: which mapping applications change most if BVLOS becomes routine? (Corridor mapping, large-area agriculture, disaster response.)

title: Assignment 1B
text:
Task
Complete one of the following two options.

Option 1: Pass the TRUST safety test
Take and pass TRUST (The Recreational UAS Safety Test), the FAA’s free online safety test for recreational flyers. The test is administered by FAA-approved test administrators, takes about 30 minutes, and cannot be failed: incorrect answers are corrected and re-asked. Keep your completion certificate; you are required to carry proof of completion whenever you fly recreationally.
Along with your certificate, write a short reflection (2 - 3 sentences): what from the training was new to you, or what surprised you the most?


Option 2: Part 107 sample questions report
Select 5 questions from the FAA’s official Part 107 sample questions and prepare a brief report that, for each question, gives the correct answer and briefly explains why it is correct (and, where useful, why the other options are wrong).
You may pick any 5 questions from the document. Choose questions that require some reasoning (airspace, charts, weather, operating rules) rather than pure recall, and use the lecture materials and the FAA study resources linked from the Part 107 guide to support your explanations.

title: Projects
text:
Proposal, presentation and paper requirements

Pre-Proposal

Submit a project pre-proposal to the project discussion forum on Moodle.

In the pre-proposal please define the scope of the project, the project location, data, and analysis you would like to perform.


Proposal

Define research question, select location, list available data, methods (theory), software tools, describe expected results.

Submit to Moodle


Presentation

Length: DE students 10 minutes, on-campus students 15 min + 5 min discussion
Introduction/background: problem, motivation for the research, research question / objective
Study site: where, why this site, geographic characteristics
Data acquisition: platform and sensor, flight plan (if applicable), flight conditions
Data properties and processing: resolution, spatial extent, accuracy
Analysis and/or modeling methods: describe methodology and workflows
Results: present and explain the results using qualitative and quantitative description, tables, graphs, maps/images
Discussion: discuss impact of flight conditions, data and methods on the results, uncertainty issues, compare with results from other studies, which questions remain unresolved, what still needs to be done
Conclusion: summary of the most important findings including advances in methodology, future work



Paper

Structure and formatting should follow scientific journal standards.
Same sections as the presentation
Text and Figures: min. 4 pages, single spaced including tables and references images, maps, graphs, presented in readable size with scale and legends where needed
References: at least 5 papers from scientific journals, rest can be reports, web documents
Appendix (optional): workflows, scripts, metadata. Software commands, issues go here

Introduction: the task and the problem
Methods: general description of the methods and concepts used
Results: the results, including maps, graphs, and tables, with comments
Discussion: anything unexpected or problematic in the results, any issues with the methodology or software, and suggestions for improvement
Conclusion: one or two sentences on what you learned

Flight Operations and Field Safety
Flight planning and execution are taught in Topic 3. Students are not required to hold a Part 107 remote pilot certificate to complete the course, and assignments can be completed with provided imagery or in simulation.
Any student who does fly is responsible for operating under FAA Part 107, including airspace authorization, visual line of sight, and altitude limits, and for following NC State policy on UAS operations on university property. Do not fly over people, do not fly a course exercise you have not planned in writing, and do not fly alone.
